title: Subnetting: CIDR and the Basics
summary: Why classful addressing wastes addresses, how CIDR enables subnetting, and how to split a network into smaller subnets.

content.body:
IPv4 addresses were originally handed out by **IANA** (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) based on company size: a very large company got a Class A or B network, a small one a Class C.

This **classful** system is rigid — Class A always /8, Class B /16, Class C /24 — and it wasted addresses:

- A **point-to-point link** between two routers only needs two addresses, but a Class C gives 256 — 252 wasted.
- A company needing 5,000 addresses had to take a Class B (~65,000) — about 60,000 wasted.

With only ~4 billion IPv4 addresses total, exhaustion became a real problem. **Subnetting** solves it by splitting larger networks into smaller ones.

**CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)** was introduced by the **IETF in 1993** to replace classful addressing. It removes the rule that Class A must be /8, Class B /16, and Class C /24, allowing prefix lengths like /25, /26, /27, and so on.

This lets a larger network be divided into **subnetworks** (subnets) sized to fit actual need. The slash notation itself (`/25`, `/26`) is called **CIDR notation**, introduced with this system. Before CIDR, only dotted-decimal masks were used.

The point-to-point link between two routers is a perfect example. Instead of using the whole `203.0.113.0/24` (254 usable addresses for 2 hosts), extend the network portion into the host bits:

- **/25** (255.255.255.128) → 7 host bits → 2⁷ − 2 = **126** usable.
- **/26** (255.255.255.192) → 6 host bits → **62** usable.
- **/27** (255.255.255.224) → 5 host bits → **30** usable.
- **/28** (255.255.255.240) → 4 host bits → **14** usable.
- **/29** (255.255.255.248) → 3 host bits → **6** usable.
- **/30** (255.255.255.252) → 2 host bits → **2** usable.

A **/30** is perfect for the link: 4 addresses total (network, R1, R2, broadcast) with zero waste. The remaining addresses (`203.0.113.4` through `.255`) stay available for other subnets.

**/31** (255.255.255.254) has only 1 host bit → 2 − 2 = **0** usable addresses, so it was historically unusable. But for a **point-to-point link** there's no need for a network or broadcast address, so both addresses can be assigned to the two routers — a /31 is valid there (Cisco shows a warning to confirm it's a point-to-point link). It's more efficient than /30.

**/32** (255.255.255.255) has no host bits and can't be used to address an interface. It does have a use later: specifying a **single host** in a static route.

sections.title: A worked example: four subnets for 45 hosts

content.body:
You have `192.168.1.0/24` and four networks of **45 hosts** each (R1's address is included in the 45). Find the smallest subnet that fits.

Each network also needs a network and broadcast address, so you need **47** addresses per subnet (45 + 2). Working through the prefix lengths:

- /30 → 2 usable — too small.
- /29 → 6 — too small.
- /28 → 14 — too small.
- /27 → 30 — too small.
- **/26 → 62 usable — fits.**

47 × 4 = 188 ≤ 256, so the /24 has enough space. (The exact subnet addresses are the subject of the next lesson.)

Remember the formula: **usable addresses = 2ⁿ − 2** where n is the **host bits**. To fit a given number of hosts, add 2 (for network + broadcast) first, then find the smallest power of two that fits. For point-to-point links, a **/30 gives 2 usable addresses** — and a **/31 is also valid** since the link needs no network/broadcast addresses.

questions.question: How many usable host addresses are in a /25 network?
questions.explanation: A /25 leaves 7 host bits. 2⁷ − 2 = 128 − 2 = 126 usable addresses.

questions.question: Which prefix length provides exactly two usable host addresses (ideal for a point-to-point link)?
questions.explanation: A /30 leaves 2 host bits: 2² − 2 = 4 − 2 = 2 usable addresses — one for each end of a point-to-point link.

questions.question: What is the dotted-decimal subnet mask for a /26 prefix length?
questions.explanation: /26 means 26 network bits. The first 24 bits are three full octets (255.255.255), plus 2 more bits in the last octet (128 + 64 = 192). So the mask is 255.255.255.192.

questions.question: Which statement about a /31 network on a point-to-point link is true?
questions.explanation: A /31 leaves only 1 host bit, so the formula gives 0 usable addresses. But on a point-to-point link there is no need for network/broadcast addresses, so both addresses can be assigned to the two routers — a /31 is valid there.

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be used under any circumstances

options.label: B
options.text: It provides 2 usable host addresses for normal LANs

options.label: C
options.text: It is valid on a point-to-point link between two routers

questions.question: You must subnet a network so each subnet can hold 45 hosts. Which prefix length should you use?
questions.explanation: Add 2 for the network and broadcast addresses → 47 needed. /26 gives 62 usable addresses (fits); /27 gives only 30 (too small).
